claim.qualifier: Tesla offers FSD as a $99/mo subscription. Marketed as 'Full Self-Driving' (without 'Supervised') from launch through January 2026.
claim.verbatim_quote: Tesla now uses the brand name 'Full Self-Driving (Supervised)' to describe its partially automated driver assistance system, and it sells it only on a subscription basis.

sources.name: Tesla — FSD product / Autopilot support page

reality.value: SAE Level 2 (driver assistance, requires constant supervision)
reality.qualifier: December 2025 California DMV administrative ruling: 'unambiguously false and counterfactual.' NHTSA opened a broad investigation in October 2025 into 2.88 million Tesla vehicles.
reality.verbatim_quote: On 'Full Self-Driving,' the court was even harsher, ruling that the name is 'actually, unambiguously false and counterfactual.'

narrative_one_liner: CA judge ruled FSD name 'unambiguously false and counterfactual' (Dec 2025); NHTSA links it to 14 crashes.
narrative: The name 'Full Self-Driving' was ruled 'unambiguously false and counterfactual' by a California administrative law judge in December 2025. Tesla's system is SAE Level 2 — driver-assistance requiring constant supervision. Tesla added '(Supervised)' to the name in January 2026 in response to the ruling, then sued the DMV in February 2026 to reverse the false-advertiser label. NHTSA's investigation links 14 crashes and 23 injuries to FSD operation.
methodology_notes: Multi-source: judicial ruling (Tier 1) + regulatory investigation (Tier 1) + media coverage (Tier 2). Both Tier-1 sources represent independent regulatory authorities (CA DMV, NHTSA).
caveats: Tesla has appealed the ruling; status as of 2026-04-25 is that Tesla complied with required name change but contests the 'false advertiser' label.
NHTSA investigation is ongoing; not all 58 incidents have been determined to be FSD-attributable.
alternative_explanations: Tesla's argument: 'Autopilot' and 'FSD' are aspirational brand names whose meaning is clarified by required user agreements. The court rejected this argument.
Some FSD incidents may be driver error rather than system failure; NHTSA investigation is examining each.
